title: Provisional review of complex-number learning milestones and affected prerequisites
status: AI-assisted preliminary desk review; educator confirmation pending
method_note: This batch reviews the edge consequences of provisionally splitting elementary algebraic complex numbers, complex-plane/polar representation, and complex analysis. The proposed checks have not been run. These are curriculum-design hypotheses, not independent expert sign-off or empirical validation.

EDGE-255: Signed/rational arithmetic supports operations on real and imaginary components across the intended basic complex-arithmetic outcome. A short local arithmetic bridge remains appropriate for learners whose only gap is calculation fluency.
Ask learners to add/subtract signed rational components and then add/subtract two a+bi numbers. Separate arithmetic errors from errors identifying real and imaginary parts.
EDGE-256: The identity i² = −1 uses integer-exponent notation, but this can be taught immediately inside the first complex-number lesson; full prior mastery of the entire powers/roots strand should not block entry.

Introduce i² = −1 locally, then test the complex-arithmetic outcome with and without a prior exponent refresher. If only exponent notation blocks progress, retain a just-in-time bridge rather than a hard gate.
EDGE-257: The mapped basic complex-number outcome includes symbolic operations and conjugate identities; expression reading and equivalence help learners expand and simplify expressions involving i. This minimum can be refreshed in the same lesson.
Ask learners to expand (a+bi)(c+di), replace i² with −1, and justify equivalent forms. Diagnose symbolic-equivalence gaps separately from complex-number meaning.
EDGE-258: The CA-003 outcome includes polar form, modulus/argument and trigonometric interpretation; unit-circle and periodic-function knowledge supplies the angle/radian and sine/cosine relationships for rectangular-to-polar conversion.

Give a complex number in rectangular form and ask the learner to find its magnitude and argument and convert to polar form. Separate coordinate/distance errors from trig-sign, quadrant, and radian errors.
EDGE-259: Complex functions and complex differentiation operate on complex inputs and outputs; elementary complex-number meaning and arithmetic are foundational to the mapped complex-analysis outcome.
Ask learners to evaluate a simple polynomial at a+bi and interpret a complex-valued function before discussing the complex derivative. Provide a CA-001 refresher if arithmetic alone is the barrier.
EDGE-260: For the current complex-differentiation outcome, elementary differentiation language and rule fluency support computing and comparing derivatives of complex-valued expressions. A formal limit-based introduction can bridge this if needed.

Compare the real derivative of x² with the formal derivative of z² and then examine the complex difference quotient. Record whether derivative notation/rules or complex-number arithmetic is the actual blocker.
EDGE-261: The mapped complex-analysis outcome includes proofs and precise assumptions; proof architecture, definitions, lemmas and conditions support the intended university/advanced depth.
Ask learners to identify assumptions and justify one short complex-differentiability claim. Test whether an explicitly scaffolded proof bridge is enough before requiring broader proof fluency.
EDGE-269: Quadratic equations motivate why complex numbers are useful when a real quadratic has no real roots, but this application is not needed to learn basic complex arithmetic. It should be an extension/link rather than a gate.
Teach basic a+bi arithmetic without a quadratic prerequisite, then use x²+1=0 as a motivation. Confirm that the core arithmetic outcomes remain achievable before the quadratic connection.
EDGE-270: Ordered pairs, axes and coordinate conventions support representing a complex number as a point with real and imaginary coordinates. A compact coordinate primer can be embedded in the CA-003 lesson.
Plot a+bi as (a,b) and read points back into algebraic form. Assess sign/axis conventions and coordinate fluency separately.
EDGE-271: Modulus is the distance from the origin, computed from the real and imaginary components using the Pythagorean theorem; polar-form magnitude therefore depends on distance reasoning for the full target outcome.
For z=a+bi, derive |z|=√(a²+b²) from a labelled right triangle and test with exact coordinates. Distinguish theorem/application errors from arithmetic errors.
EDGE-272: The geometry/polar cluster builds directly on understanding a+bi and component-wise operations; it then interprets those numbers as points/vectors and connects multiplication with transformations.
Teach a+bi and conjugates first, then plot, compute modulus/argument, and compare multiplication with a geometric rotation/scaling example. Check the algebraic and geometric skills separately.
EDGE-273: Polar/geometric interpretation is valuable in complex analysis but is not universally necessary for the definition of complex differentiability or an initial limit-based treatment. Keep it available as a bridge and representation, not a rigid gate for every complex-analysis entry route.

Introduce complex differentiation on a simple function using the difference quotient, then add a polar/geometric interpretation task. If the first outcome is achieved without prior polar form, keep CA-003 as helpful rather than core.
